A Keio University graduate who entered Japan's National Diet in 1963, this politician served as prime minister from 1996 to 1998 before resigning after a coalition election defeat — who is he?

Ryutaro Hashimoto: Prime Minister of Japan from 1996 to 1998. Ryutaro Hashimoto (橋本 龍太郎, Hashimoto Ryūtarō; 29 July 1937 – 1 July 2006) was a Japanese politician who served as prime minister of Japan from 1996 to 1998.
Married into the Kennedy family and the driving force behind the creation of the Peace Corps, this 1972 Democratic vice-presidential nominee also founded Head Start and Job Corps — who is he?
Sargent Shriver: American diplomat, politician and activist (1915–2011)
Born in 1940, she is the eldest child of the last Shah of Iran and his first wife, Fawzia of Egypt — who is she?

It began as a Cold War quarrel over how to read Marx — Mao branding Moscow's de-Stalinization and 'peaceful coexistence' as revisionism — and slowly froze relations between two communist giants. What is this rift called?
Names of the days of the week
Racial segregation in the United States
Sino-Soviet split: Conflict between communist blocs.
In 1956, Britain, France, and Israel jointly invaded Egypt after Nasser nationalized a vital canal — what is this conflict commonly called?
Suez Crisis: 1956 British–French–Israeli invasion of Egypt.
Named to the Time 100 "Heroes" list, this ethologist transformed humane livestock handling and was among the first autistic people to publish insights from her own experience — who is she?
Temple Grandin: American academic and autism activist (born 1947)

Nominated in 2019 by Alexander Gauland to become co-chair of Germany's far-right AfD alongside Alice Weidel, this Bundestag member is known for pro-Russian, eurosceptic foreign-policy views. Who is he?

Formed after the Napoleonic Wars by fusing the old Dutch Republic, the Austrian-ruled Low Countries, and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège into a buffer state under William I of Orange-Nassau, this polity collapsed with the 1830 Belgian Revolution — what was it called?
United Kingdom of the Netherlands: European territory (1815–1839)

His brother was executed for revolutionary activities in 1887, pushing him toward radical politics. He founded the Bolsheviks, led the October Revolution, and created the world's first communist state—then ruled it until his death in 1924. Who was this Russian revolutionary?
Vladimir Lenin: Leader of the Soviet Union from 1922 to 1924.
Introduced to the public in 1954 by a retired British civil servant, this modern pagan, Earth-focused religion blends ancient motifs with 20th-century hermetic ideas — which religion?
Wicca: Modern syncretic pagan religion. Wicca draws upon ancient pagan and 20th-century hermetic motifs for theological and ritual purposes.
This 7th-century Chinese Buddhist monk journeyed to the Indian subcontinent from 629 to 645 CE and brought back more than 650 Sanskrit texts to translate — who is he?
Xuanzang: Chinese Buddhist monk and scholar (602–664)
Born into poverty and adopted by a wealthy uncle, this Chinese general commanded the Eighth Route Army and is regarded as a principal founder of the People's Republic. Who was he?
Zhu De: Chinese general and politician (1886–1976)
Which of these people was born first?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four began earliest?
Python (programming language) (founded 1991) is the earliest of the four. Python supports multiple programming paradigms but with an emphasis on object-oriented programming and dynamic typing.
Which one below was established earliest?
MATLAB (founded 1984) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
Robert Boyle is a physicist. Robert Boyle (25 January 1627 – 31 December 1691) was an Anglo-Irish natural philosopher, chemist, physicist, alchemist and inventor.
Pick the chemist from these four.
James Lovelock is a chemist. James Ephraim Lovelock (26 July 1919 – 26 July 2022) was an English independent scientist, environmentalist and futurist.
What is the atomic number of Neodymium?
Neodymium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nd and atomic number 60.
In what year was Pythagoras born?
Pythagoras: Pythagoras of Samos (Ancient Greek: Πυθαγόρας; c. 570 – c. 495 BC) was an ancient Ionian Greek philosopher, polymath, and the eponymous founder of Pythagoreanism.
In what year was Elon Musk born?
Elon Musk: Elon Reeve Musk (EE-lon; born June 28, 1971) is a businessman and former public official who is the CEO and largest shareholder of Tesla and SpaceX.
In what year was Armin Meiwes born?
Armin Meiwes: After Meiwes and the victim jointly attempted to eat the victim's severed penis, Meiwes murdered his victim and proceeded to eat a large amount of his flesh.
In what year did Mohamed Atta die?
Mohamed Atta: In Hamburg, Atta attended prayers at the al-Quds Mosque where he met Marwan al-Shehhi, Ramzi bin al-Shibh, and Ziad Jarrah, with whom he formed the Hamburg cell.
In what year did Nostradamus die?
Nostradamus's father's family had originally been Jewish, but had converted to Catholic Christianity a generation before Nostradamus was born.
In what year was Silver discovered?
Silver is a chemical element; it has symbol Ag (from Latin argentum 'silver') and atomic number 47.
In what year was Manganese discovered?
Manganese is a chemical element; it has the symbol Mn and atomic number 25.
Which company manufactures LTV A-7 Corsair II?
LTV A-7 Corsair II: Ling-Temco-Vought. The LTV A-7 Corsair II is an American carrier-capable subsonic light attack aircraft designed and manufactured by Ling-Temco-Vought (LTV).
Which country is Sukhoi Su-57 from?
Sukhoi Su-57: Russia. The Sukhoi Su-57 (Russian: Сухой Су-57; NATO reporting name: Felon) is a twin-engine stealth multirole fighter aircraft developed by Sukhoi.
Who is credited with discovering Grus?
Grus (constellation): Petrus Plancius. Grus (or colloquially) is a constellation in the southern sky.
Who is credited with discovering Reynolds number?
Reynolds number: Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet. At low Reynolds numbers, flows tend to be dominated by laminar (sheet-like) flow, while at high Reynolds numbers, flows tend to be turbulent.
Who is credited with discovering Ceres?
Ceres (dwarf planet): Giuseppe Piazzi. Ceres is a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
This localized collection of pus builds up within body tissue, usually from bacterial infection, causing redness, pain, warmth, and swelling. What is it?
Abscess is a collection of pus that has built up within the tissue of the body, usually caused by bacterial infection.
A pioneer of industrial toxicology, this American physician trained at Michigan, worked out of Hull House in Chicago, and led the fight to curb lead poisoning in the workplace — who was she?
Alice Hamilton (February 27, 1869 - September 22, 1970) was an American physician, research scientist, and author.

Native to tropical America and carried across the Pacific by Spanish traders aboard the Manila galleons, this small tree in the same family as soursop produces a scaly-skinned fruit with sweet, creamy flesh — what's the species?
Annona squamosa is a small, well-branched tree or shrub from the family Annonaceae that bears edible fruits called sugar apples or sweetsops or custard apples.

Explicitly describing the relativity of motion and, by his own account, 23 years old in 499 CE, this figure is considered the first of the great mathematician-astronomers of classical Indian science — who is he?
Aryabhata (476-550 CE) was the first of the major mathematician-astronomers and early physicist from the classical age of Indian mathematics and Indian astronomy.

An Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean, it is one of two living members of the family Monodontidae and is also known as the white whale (the only cetacean regularly occurring with this color) and the sea canary for its high-pitched calls. What is it?
Beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas), is an Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean.
This leafy vegetable forms no head, just green blades atop pale bulbous stalks, with a flavor often compared to a mix of spinach and water chestnut — what vegetable is it?

Bok choy (American English, Canadian English, and Australian English), pak choi (British English, South African English, and Caribbean English) or pok choi is a type of Chinese cabbage (Brassica rapa subsp.
Unlike ordinary weight loss from undereating, this illness-linked syndrome strips away muscle mass in ways good nutrition can't fully undo — what condition is it?
Cachexia is a syndrome that occurs in people with certain illnesses, causing muscle loss that cannot be fully reversed with improved nutrition.
This clouding of the eye's lens is responsible for nearly 40 percent of blindness cases worldwide, often causing halos around lights and trouble seeing at night — what condition is it?
Cataract is a cloudy area in the lens of the eye that impairs vision.
Linked to repeated head trauma, this worsening neurodegenerative disease turns up in boxers and footballers — and even in soccer players, largely from heading the ball. What is it?

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a neurodegenerative disease linked to repeated trauma to the head. The encephalopathy symptoms can include behavioral problems, mood problems, and problems with thinking.
This group of mostly evergreen, cone-bearing trees and shrubs reproduces via wind-pollination, with the seeds themselves also scattered by the wind — what plant group is it?
Conifer are a group of vascular plants and a subset of gymnosperms.
Native to Mexico and Central America and related to the sunflower and daisy, this genus of 49 tuberous perennial species blooms in nearly every color except blue — which genus?
Dahlia is a genus of bushy, tuberous, herbaceous perennial plants native to Mexico and Central America.
Tamed in Africa millennia ago and still hauling loads across the developing world, which equine traces its lineage to Equus africanus?
Donkey is a domesticated equine. It was domesticated in Africa some 5000–7000 years ago, and has been used mainly as a working animal since that time.
Born to a mathematician father in Erlangen, this pioneering algebraist proved theorems connecting symmetry to conservation laws in physics — who is she?
Emmy Noether (23 March 1882 - 14 April 1935) was a German mathematician who made many important contributions to abstract algebra.

This front-of-the-head feature found in humans and other animals houses most of the sense organs, including the eyes, nose, and mouth, and its damage can profoundly affect one's sense of identity — name this body part?
Face is the front of the head in humans and many other animals that features most of the sense organs including the eyes, nose and mouth.
This Italian-American economist, who taught at MIT's Sloan School, took home the 1985 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics. Who was he?
Franco Modigliani (18 June 1918 - 25 September 2003) was an Italian-American economist and the recipient of the 1985 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics.

He shared a 1951 Nobel for synthesizing ten transuranium elements and developed the actinide concept that reshaped the periodic table; this American chemist later advised ten US presidents on nuclear policy — who was he?

Glenn T. Seaborg (April 19, 1912 - February 25, 1999) was an American chemist whose involvement in the synthesis, discovery and investigation of ten transuranium elements earned him a share of the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Prehensile and multi-fingered, this appendage sits at the end of primates' forearms, though a few other animals like koalas and raccoons are sometimes described as having one too — which body part?
Hand is a prehensile, multi-fingered appendage located at the end of the forearm or forelimb of primates such as humans, chimpanzees, monkeys, and lemurs.
Originally a variable measure equal to one-twelfth of the night or day in the ancient Near East, this unit of time is now fixed at exactly 3,600 seconds — name this unit?
Hour (symbol: h; also abbreviated hr) is a unit of time historically reckoned as 124 of a day and defined contemporarily as exactly 3,600 seconds.
This contagious bacterial skin infection most often shows up as yellowish crusts on a child's face, arms, or legs, and spreads easily in crowded day cares and contact sports — what is it?
Impetigo is a contagious bacterial infection that involves the superficial skin.

This Swiss psychologist's theory of cognitive development, paired with his epistemological views, is together known as genetic epistemology, and remains foundational in early-childhood education. Who is he?
Jean Piaget (9 August 1896 - 16 September 1980) was a Swiss psychologist known for his work on child development.
Arrested in 1995 for various computer crimes and imprisoned for five years, this convicted hacker later became a computer-security consultant and author — who is he?
Kevin Mitnick (August 6, 1963 - July 16, 2023) was an American computer security consultant, author, and convicted hacker.
This bacterial blood infection, spread between humans, dogs, and rodents, can range from symptomless to a severe form that turns skin and eyes yellow and shuts down the kidneys — what disease is it?
Leptospirosis is a blood infection caused by bacteria of the genus Leptospira that can infect humans, dogs, rodents, and many other wild and domesticated animals.
Born in Vienna into one of Europe's richest families, this philosopher studied under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge and transformed 20th-century philosophy of language and logic — who is he?

Ludwig Wittgenstein ((h)tyne; Austrian; 26 April 1889 - 29 April 1951) was an Austro-British philosopher who worked in logic, philosophy of mathematics, philosophy of mind, and philosophy of language.
Often called the 'father of the handheld cell phone,' this Motorola engineer placed the first public mobile call in 1973 from a New York City sidewalk — who is he?
Martin Cooper (inventor) (born December 26, 1928) is an American engineer.

An advanced modification of the Korean War-era MiG-15, this Soviet transonic fighter jet entered production in 1952, was license-built in both China and Poland, and remains in North Korean service today — what's the aircraft?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-17 (NATO reporting name: Fresco) is a transonic fighter aircraft that was produced in the Soviet Union from 1952 and was operated by air forces internationally.
Caused by antibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, this autoimmune disease most often weakens the muscles of the eyes, face and throat — which disease?
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a long-term neuromuscular junction disease that leads to varying degrees of skeletal muscle weakness.

Made from unleavened dough rolled flat and then cut, stretched, or extruded into long strips, this staple food appears across cultures — in Italian cuisine, it goes by an entirely different name. What is it, generically?
Noodle are a type of food typically made from unleavened dough which is rolled flat and cut, stretched, or extruded into long strips or strings.
Dubbed the father of nuclear chemistry, he studied under Ernest Rutherford before helping identify the radioactive elements radium, thorium, and protactinium — who is he?
Otto Hahn (8 March 1879 - 28 July 1968) was a German chemist who was a pioneer in the field of radiochemistry.

A Chinese singer famous for annual appearances on a widely watched Lunar New Year television gala, she has served as her country's First Lady since 2012 as the wife of its paramount leader — who is she?

Peng Liyuan (pinyin: Png Lyun; born 20 November 1962) is a Chinese singer who has served as the First Lady of China since 2012, as the wife of Xi Jinping, the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party and paramount leader of China.
Which condition, more common in people with obesity or a family history, involves hair and skin debris being drawn into tissue through tiny skin openings called pits?
Pilonidal disease is a type of skin infection that typically occurs as a cyst between the cheeks of the buttocks and often at the upper end.
Used to disinfect both healthcare workers' hands and patients' skin before and after surgery, this antiseptic can be applied as a liquid, ointment, or powder — which compound?

Povidone-iodine is an antiseptic used for skin disinfection before and after surgery. Povidone-iodine (PVP-I), also known as iodopovidone, is an antiseptic used for skin disinfection before and after surgery.
Used to treat malaria and babesiosis, this medication also gives tonic water its distinctive bitter taste — what is it?
Quinine is a medication used to treat malaria and babesiosis. While sometimes used for nocturnal leg cramps, quinine is not recommended for this purpose due to the risk of serious side effects.
One of the U.S. Air Force's three strategic bombers, this supersonic swing-wing aircraft hauls a 75,000-pound payload and answers to the affectionate name 'Bone' — what is it?
Rockwell B-1 Lancer is a supersonic variable-sweep wing, heavy bomber used by the United States Air Force.
Which genus of large, tropical, many-legged predators takes its name from ancient Greek words meaning roughly 'thorn' and 'earthworm'?
Scolopendra (from Ancient Greek (sklops), meaning "thorn", and (nteron), meaning "earthworm") is a species-rich genus of large tropical centipedes of the family Scolopendridae.
This structural framework supporting an animal's body comes in three main forms — a rigid outer shell, a rigid inner frame, or a flexible fluid-supported structure — what is it called?
Skeleton is the structural frame that supports the body of most animals.
Also known as sea stars, roughly 1,900 species of these star-shaped marine invertebrates live on seabeds from warm tropics to icy polar oceans. What are they?
Starfish are a class of marine invertebrates generally shaped like a star polygon.
Though some scientists place it in its own genus, Acrocodia, the Malayan species is usually still classified within this genus of tapir — name this genus?
Tapirus is a genus of tapir which contains the living tapir species.
This genus of about 30 tree and shrub species is native across the temperate Northern Hemisphere, with its greatest diversity found in Asia — what genus is it?
Tilia is a genus of about 30 species of trees or bushes, native throughout most of the temperate Northern Hemisphere.
Nicknamed carbamide, this is the simplest amide of carbamic acid: two amino groups joined by a single carbonyl, and the body's chief way of shedding nitrogen in urine. What compound is it?
Urea (because it is a diamide of carbonic acid), is an organic compound with chemical formula CO(NH2)2.
This German hunting-dog breed, recognized in 1891, is so much a working dog that in its homeland it's considered unsuitable simply as a house pet — name the breed?
Weimaraner is a German breed of hunting dog of medium to large size, with history going back at least to the nineteenth century.
Discovered in 1807 and named for the Roman goddess of home and hearth, this is thought to be the second-largest asteroid and the only known rocky protoplanet still intact in the belt — which one?
4 Vesta: Second largest main-belt asteroid. Vesta (minor-planet designation: 4 Vesta) is one of the largest objects in the asteroid belt, with a mean diameter of 525 kilometres (326 mi).
Native to sub-Saharan grasslands and woodlands, this animal is the largest living land species, with the largest recorded specimen standing nearly 13 feet tall at the shoulder — which species is it?
African bush elephant: Species of mammal. Its skin is grey with scanty hairs, and bending cracks which support thermoregulation by retaining water.

Its seasonal form is called hay fever: a type I hypersensitivity reaction where the immune system overreacts to airborne allergens, bringing sneezing, a runny nose, and itchy, watery eyes — what's the medical name?
Allergic rhinitis: Nasal inflammation due to allergens in the air.
This scientific discipline uses techniques from titration to mass spectrometry to identify unknown compounds and measure exactly how much of each substance is present in a mixture - which field?
Analytical chemistry: Study of the separation, identification, and quantification of matter.
When an injury to the wall of the body's main artery lets blood force its layers apart, victims often feel a sudden 'tearing' chest or back pain — what's this medical emergency called?
Aortic dissection: Injury to the innermost layer of the aorta.
Born from acetylsalicylic acid, this everyday drug cools fevers within about 30 minutes and is taken long-term to fend off heart attacks and strokes by quieting platelets — what is it?
One of the first grains ever domesticated, around 9000 BC in the Fertile Crescent, this cereal now ranks fourth in world production — and 70% of it goes to feeding animals — what is it?
Barley: Cereal grain. Barley (Hordeum vulgare), a member of the grass family, is a major cereal grain grown in temperate climates globally.
Before becoming TV's most famous bow-tied science educator, this Boeing mechanical engineer invented a hydraulic resonance suppressor tube for 747s, then quit to do sketch comedy. Who is he?

A twin-engine, carrier-capable strike fighter flown by the U.S., Australia, and Kuwait, this larger, more advanced follow-on to an earlier 1980s Navy jet packs an internal 20 mm rotary cannon and can be rigged as an airborne refueling tanker — what is it called?
The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom
Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet: Series of carrier-based multirole combat aircraft.
Despite the name, this pseudocereal isn't related to true cereals at all — it's kin to rhubarb and sorrel, and was first cultivated in Yunnan around 6,000 BC — which crop is it?
Buckwheat: Species of flowering plant in the family Polygonaceae.
This suborder of 'dog-like' carnivores includes bears, raccoons, weasels, and seals, and is thought to have diversified mainly across North America and northern Eurasia — what's it called?
Caniformia: Suborder of mammals. Caniformia is a suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of "dog-like" carnivorans.
Named for barbels that resemble a cat's whiskers, these scaleless, ray-finned fish include giants like the Mekong species and go by nicknames such as 'mud cat' in the Southern US — what are they?
Catfish: Order of fish. Catfish are a diverse group of ray-finned fish of the order Siluriformes (historically Nematognathi).

One of the earliest cultivated legumes — its oldest traces were unearthed in Syria — this protein-packed seed goes by names like garbanzo and chana, and forms the backbone of hummus and falafel. What is it?
Chickpea: Species of flowering plant with edible seeds.
This English inventor made the world's first slimline pocket calculator in 1972, then launched the UK's first mass-market home computer for under £100 — who is he?
Clive Sinclair: English entrepreneur and inventor (1940–2021)
A heavy-set, fox-like canid native to East Asia, this animal is named for its raccoon-like face markings and is unusual among canids for hibernating in winter and climbing trees. What is this animal?
Common raccoon dog: Canid indigenous to East Asia. Named for its raccoon-like face markings, it is most closely related to foxes.

An incurable, always fatal neurodegenerative disease belonging to the transmissible spongiform encephalopathy group, it causes early symptoms like memory problems, behavioral changes, and poor coordination, with about 70% of sufferers dying within a year. What disease is it?
Known as Queen Anne's lace, this Old World wildflower is the wild ancestor of the cultivated carrot — what is it?
Daucus carota: Species of flowering plant.
A Cambridge-educated lecturer in English literature, this Hashemite princess briefly reigned as Queen of Jordan as King Hussein's first wife — who is she?
Dina bint Abdul-Hamid: Queen of Jordan from 1955 to 1957.
Known as 'crawling' pinnipeds to distinguish them from their eared, sea-lion-like cousins, this group's only completely freshwater population lives in Lake Baikal — what are they called?
Affecting roughly 10% of women of reproductive age — nearly 200 million worldwide — this disease occurs when tissue like the uterine lining grows on the ovaries, bowel, or elsewhere. What is it?

Exercise, laughter, dancing, and romantic love can all trigger this intense state of well-being via the brain's pleasure centers — though it's also a symptom of mania and the lure of addictive drugs. What is it?
Euphoria: Intense feelings of well-being. Euphoria (yoo-FOR-ee-ə) is the experience (or affect) of pleasure or excitement and intense feelings of well-being and happiness.
A founder of modern topology who also wrote under the playful pen name "Paul Mongré," this German mathematician — Jewish and facing deportation — died by suicide with his family in 1942. Who was he?
Felix Hausdorff: German mathematician (1868–1942). Hausdorff was Jewish, and life became difficult for him and his family after the Kristallnacht of 1938.

Present in about 80% of adults as harmless white or yellow bumps on the lips, cheeks, or gums, these visible sebaceous glands were first described in 1896 by an American dermatologist — what are they called?
Fordyce spots: Sebaceous glands that are present in most individuals.

In 1974 in Pacific Grove, California, this computer scientist demoed the first working prototype of CP/M and invented the BIOS, then founded Digital Research to sell his software — who was this PC-revolution pioneer?
Gary Kildall: American computer scientist and microcomputer entrepreneur (1942–1994)
This American chemist helped synthesize ten transuranium elements, dreamed up the actinide concept, and advised ten US presidents on nuclear policy — who shared the 1951 Nobel for that work?
Closely related to the llama, this wild South American camelid shares its range with a higher-altitude cousin, the vicuña — what is it?
Named for the Greek word for the sun, this element makes up about 24% of the universe's elemental mass and has the lowest boiling point of all — which colorless, odorless gas?
Helium: Chemical element with atomic number 2 (He)
Nicknamed 'handy man' for its toolmaking, this archaic human species lived in East and South Africa as far back as 2.4 million years ago — which species?
Homo habilis: Archaic human species from 2.4 to 1.65 mya.

Typically begun with an induction of preliminary instructions, this state of focused attention and heightened suggestibility is debated as either an altered trance or a form of imaginative role-play — what is it?
Hypnosis: State of increased suggestibility. There are competing theories explaining hypnosis and related phenomena.

This analytical framework describes how overlapping identities like race, gender, and class combine to create unique experiences of discrimination or privilege, and emerged partly as a critique of mainstream feminism — which concept?
Intersectionality: Theory of discrimination. The term intersectionality was coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989.
A French soldier turned naturalist, this early proponent of biological evolution published the three-volume 'Flore françoise' and joined the French Academy of Sciences in 1779 — who is he?
Nicknamed 'Iron Annie,' which corrugated-skin transport plane began life as a 1930 civilian airliner before Nazi Germany converted it for military use?
Biosynthesized in the body from the amino acid tyrosine, this compound is the direct precursor to dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine — what is it?
L-DOPA: Chemical compound. As is true for many molecules, the human body produces only one of these isomers (the l-DOPA form).
Born in Germany, this businessman founded the first company to manufacture blue jeans, beginning operations in San Francisco in 1853 — who is he?
Marketed as Imodium, this opioid-class medication treats diarrhea without crossing the blood-brain barrier at normal doses?
Loperamide: Medicine used to reduce diarrhea.
Males of this widespread dabbling duck species sport iridescent green heads, while females have brown-speckled plumage — which bird?
Mallard: Species of duck. The mallard or wild duck (Anas platyrhynchos) is a dabbling duck that breeds throughout the temperate and subtropical Americas, Eurasia, and North Africa.

Selected in 1969 as a dedicated air-superiority fighter and first flown in 1972, this twin-engine American jet boasts a staggering combat record of 106 victories and zero losses — which aircraft is it?
McDonnell Douglas F-15 Eagle: Multirole and air superiority fighter family.

Born from the French Revolution's push to standardize units into the metric system, this scientific field oversees everything from the SI unit system to the labs that keep rulers honest — what is it called?
Metrology: Science of measurement and its application.
Its dust-like, colored, fuzzy appearance on food comes from spores, and its branching network of hyphae — called a mycelium — counts as a single organism; what fungal structure is this?
Mold: Wooly, dust-like fungal structure or substance.
This symbiotic partnership between fungus and plant roots plays a crucial role in plant nutrition and soil chemistry — usually mutualistic, but sometimes parasitic. What's the association called?
Mycorrhiza: Fungus-plant symbiotic association. The term mycorrhiza refers to the role of the fungus in the plant's rhizosphere, the plant root system and its surroundings.

This silvery-white transition metal with a faint golden tinge resists corrosion thanks to a thin oxide layer, and in pure native form it's mostly found inside iron meteorites — which element, atomic number 28, is it?
Nickel: Chemical element with atomic number 28 (Ni)
First described by Linnaeus in 1758, this medium-sized spotted wild cat hunts armadillos and opossums at twilight across a range from the southwestern US to South America — what cat is it?
Ocelot: Species of wild cat. It is native to the southwestern United States, Mexico, Central and South America, and the Caribbean islands of Trinidad and Margarita.

Triggered by a surge of luteinizing hormone near the midpoint of the menstrual cycle, this event sees the ovarian follicle rupture and release an egg — which breaks down in under a day if it isn't fertilized. What is it called?
Ovulation: Release of egg cells from the ovaries.
One of the 20th century's most prolific mathematicians, this Hungarian championed Ramsey theory and famously preferred cracking open problems to building grand theories — who was he?
Sold under the brand name Luminal, this WHO-recommended barbiturate treats epilepsy in children and can be given intravenously for status epilepticus — which drug?
Phenobarbital: Medication of the barbiturate type.
Injected by a mosquito's bite and multiplying first in the liver before invading red blood cells, this parasite genus is the cause of malaria — what is it?
Plasmodium: Genus of parasitic protists that can cause malaria.
Originating in Spain's Canary Islands, this large mastiff-type breed was historically used for guarding, herding sheep and cattle, and — legally until 1936 — dog fighting. Which breed?
Presa Canario: Spanish breed of dog. It originates in the Spanish autonomous community of the Canary Islands, and is found mostly in the islands of Gran Canaria and Tenerife.
This white-yellow-brown fluid forms at sites of infection, and when trapped in an enclosed tissue space, it creates what's known as an abscess — what is it called?
Pus: Fluid produced by inflammatory infection.

Named after a 19th-century British naturalist employed by the East India Company, this small deer species native to south-eastern China and Taiwan has also become an established wild population in the UK and Ireland — what is it?
Reeves's muntjac: Species of deer. It has also been introduced in the United Kingdom, Ireland, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Japan.
Grown in South Africa's Fynbos biome, this caffeine-free herbal infusion has an earthy flavor similar to yerba mate and carries protected designation of origin status in the EU. What is it?
Rooibos: Species of plant in the family Fabaceae.

This Harvard political scientist coordinated security planning for Jimmy Carter's National Security Council, but he's best remembered for a 1993 theory arguing future wars would be fought between cultures rather than countries — who was he?
Samuel P. Huntington: American political scientist and academic (1927–2008)
This secretive Soviet chief designer built the rocket that launched the first satellite, the first animal in orbit, and the first human into space — who was he?
Lose your coiled shell entirely and you're called a slug; keep one big enough to retract into and you're this shelled gastropod instead — what creature?
Snail: Shelled gastropod. The name is most often applied to land snails, terrestrial pulmonate gastropod molluscs.
This rodent family includes tree-dwelling, ground-dwelling, and gliding members like chipmunks and prairie dogs, and traces its fossil record back to the Eocene epoch — which animal family?
Squirrel: Family of rodents. The squirrel family includes tree squirrels, ground squirrels (including chipmunks and prairie dogs, among others), and flying squirrels.
